questions.question: Which metric does the Automatic Database Diagnostic Monitor (ADDM) center its performance analysis around to evaluate the impact of system bottlenecks?

answerOptions.rationale: ADDM quantifies performance issues based on the percentage of total non-idle session call time accumulated by the database.
Elapsed Time represents total wall-clock time between snapshots, whereas ADDM specifically targets non-idle database session activity.
Redo generation rate reflects transactional throughput but is not the core metric ADDM uses to rank bottleneck impact.
Hard parsing rates highlight library cache efficiency, but ADDM evaluates overall system impact through session work duration.

questions.hint: Consider the key metric that combines CPU time and non-idle wait time across active session calls.

questions.question: Which Oracle background process is responsible for periodically flushing Active Session History (ASH) in-memory data into AWR repository tables on disk?

answerOptions.rationale: The Memory Monitor process automatically transfers sampled active session data from SGA ring buffers to disk tables during snapshot operations.
LGWR handles flushing redo log buffer contents to online redo log files, not SGA performance telemetry.
DBWR writes modified data blocks from the SGA buffer cache to physical data files.
RVWR is dedicated to writing flashback database logs when Flashback Database is enabled.

questions.hint: Identify the background process dedicated to managing background performance diagnostics and repository statistics.

questions.question: Which SQL*Plus diagnostic script generates an AWR Compare Period report for single-instance Oracle environments to evaluate performance changes across patch updates?

answerOptions.rationale: This script prompts for two distinct snapshot pairs to generate a side-by-side performance delta report in single-instance databases.
This specific script variation is designed for Real Application Clusters (RAC) environments rather than single-instance databases.
This script generates an ADDM root-cause analysis report for a single pair of AWR snapshots rather than comparing two distinct operational windows.
This standard script generates a baseline AWR report for a single snapshot range rather than a comparative diff between two windows.

questions.hint: Look for the standard reporting script name containing 'dd' to signify double-differential analysis for single instances.

questions.question: What sampling interval does Active Session History (ASH) use to record active database session details inside the SGA ring buffer?

answerOptions.rationale: ASH samples active sessions every second in memory, making it effective for catching transient performance spikes.
Hourly intervals correspond to the default frequency of AWR snapshots rather than real-time ASH sampling.
Ten-second intervals smooth out transient spikes that ASH's finer sampling granularity is designed to capture.
While granular, ASH's actual in-memory sampling engine runs at a faster frequency.

questions.hint: Think about the sub-minute rate needed to catch brief I/O or locking bottlenecks.

questions.question: When diagnosing user I/O issues, which wait event typically signifies single-block data reads associated with index lookups or nested loop join operations?

answerOptions.rationale: Single-block access paths reading contiguous index or table blocks generate this specific wait event.
This event indicates multi-block read operations typically associated with full table scans.
This event indicates read operations that bypass the SGA buffer cache directly into session PGA memory.
This wait event indicates session contention when attempting to access a block currently pinned or read by another session.

questions.hint: Recall the wait event name used when blocks are read one by one sequentially into memory.

questions.question: Which database wait event is raised when multiple sessions attempt to update or delete the same rows concurrently without committing?

answerOptions.rationale: Transaction enqueues in row lock mode occur when a session waits for another uncommitted transaction to release its row lock.
This event relates to space management allocation in dictionary-managed tablespaces.
This latch event indicates memory-level contention for hot blocks in the buffer cache hash buckets.
This event controls object execution concurrency in the shared pool rather than application row locks.

questions.hint: Focus on the transaction enqueue event associated with row-level locking.

questions.question: Exceeding which initialization parameter limit results in an ORA-00020 error in Oracle Database?

answerOptions.rationale: The static processes parameter caps total OS user processes connecting to the database; reaching this limit triggers ORA-00020.
Exceeding the open_cursors per-session limit raises ORA-01000 rather than ORA-00020.
Reaching SGA memory boundaries leads to allocation errors such as ORA-04031 rather than process rejection errors.
PGA target limits cause work areas to spill to temporary tablespaces rather than rejecting new connection processes.

questions.hint: Select the static parameter that governs instance-wide operating system connection slots.

questions.question: Which dynamic function call in the DBMS_XPLAN package allows a DBA to inspect runtime execution plan metrics, comparing Estimated Rows (E-Rows) against Actual Rows (A-Rows)?

answerOptions.rationale: Using DISPLAY_CURSOR with the 'ALLSTATS LAST' format retrieves actual runtime row counts and execution statistics directly from memory.
DISPLAY_AWR formats historical execution plans stored on disk rather than active cursor statistics from the SGA.
DISPLAY_SQLSET extracts plans stored within a SQL Tuning Set rather than runtime memory cursors.
GATHER_TABLE_STATS collects schema statistics for the optimizer rather than displaying query execution plans.

questions.hint: Identify the function used to fetch cursor plans directly out of the shared SQL area.

questions.question: Which initialization parameter sets an instance-wide limit for non-shared memory allocated to session work areas such as sort operations and hash joins?

answerOptions.rationale: This parameter establishes an instance-wide target for total private process memory allocated across active database sessions.
sga_target manages shared memory structures including the buffer cache and shared pool.
open_cursors defines the maximum statement handle count a single session can maintain simultaneously.
db_cache_size specifies memory allocated exclusively to caching data blocks within the SGA.

questions.hint: Look for the aggregate target parameter that controls Program Global Area allocations.

questions.question: As a general rule of thumb, how much free disk space should be provisioned at the auxiliary destination during an RMAN Table Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)?

answerOptions.text: Space for SYSTEM + SYSAUX + active UNDO + the target tablespace (approx. 2x the target tablespace)
answerOptions.rationale: RMAN table PITR provisions an auxiliary instance requiring core system tablespaces alongside the tablespace housing the recovered table.

answerOptions.text: Space equal to 10% of the entire database backup size
answerOptions.rationale: Auxiliary space depends on specific tablespace data file sizes rather than a percentage of total database backups.

answerOptions.text: Space equal to the SGA and PGA memory parameters combined
answerOptions.rationale: Auxiliary destination requirements dictate physical disk storage for data files rather than instance memory allocation limits.

answerOptions.text: Space strictly equal to the size of the dropped table's export dump
answerOptions.rationale: RMAN must reconstruct systemic data files during recovery, requiring significantly more space than just the target table.

questions.hint: Consider all the system and undo data files required to create an auxiliary database instance alongside the target table's tablespace.
